clue.text: Make provision in a flexible way

definitions.meaning: to provide or furnish what is needed
an adverb from supple: in a pliant, bendy manner

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the rare adverb of supple (supple-ly), pronounced differently from the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means furnish or provide, and the adverb means pliantly, formed from supple.

clue.text: Dave's tie retied — that'll calm him

indicators.note: a tie tied again is rearranged, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: Dave's supplies its S as a letter here

explanation.surface: Dave fusses with his tie until he feels calmer.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug that soothes or tranquillises a patient.

clue.text: Hands in our arms? On the contrary

definitions.text: Hands in our arms? On the contrary

parts.words: Hands in our arms? On the contrary
parts.note: turn it round: arms held in our hands, that is handguns

explanation.surface: A question about embracing, then a contradiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Reversing the phrase gives 'arms in our hands': weapons held in the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Handguns are firearms carried in one hand.

clue.text: Rather slow movement right in the French quarter

indicators.note: in places the letter for right inside the other pieces

parts.note: la is the French feminine for the
a ghetto is a city quarter where a group lives

explanation.surface: Someone moves slowly and to the right inside the French quarter of a city.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical piece or section in a tempo a little less slow than largo.

clue.text: Where good training bears fruit

parts.note: read literally: a lattice on which fruit trees are trained flat against a wall, so careful training yields a crop

explanation.surface: A proverb that discipline pays off in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: This lattice or trellis is the frame against which fruit trees are trained to grow flat.

clue.text: Wheelbase-a paper's motoring feature?

parts.note: read as the base of a car's wheel, and as a newspaper column about driving

explanation.surface: A newspaper's car page discusses the distance between axles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wheelbase' is a car term for axle spacing; here it is what the steering wheel sits on, and 'paper's feature' is a regular column.
explanation.definitionFit: The shaft that holds the steering wheel, and a press column on driving.

clue.text: Fiery cross ?

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiery cross' looks like the burning signal of a Scottish clan; the words are two separate synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean irate: a fiery temper, a cross mood.

clue.text: Encourage Jack in top place in his job

definitions.meaning: to fill with enthusiasm or stimulate

definitions.text: Jack in top place in his job
definitions.meaning: a steeplejack at work is up in the spire, the top of the steeple

explanation.surface: A worker is urged on to reach the top of his trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the answer as IN SPIRE: a steeplejack does his job up a spire.
explanation.definitionFit: To stimulate or encourage someone; and a steeplejack working at the top is in a spire.

clue.text: Singer in trouble with the Opposition !

indicators.note: a word in trouble is disturbed, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A political singer gets in hot water for siding with the Opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: A minister who quits the government leaves office and may end up voting with the other side.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister who quits office leaves the government benches and may join its opponents.

clue.text: Better prospects here for railway' travellers

definitions.text: Better prospects here for railway' travellers

parts.words: Better prospects here for railway' travellers
parts.note: prospects as views: a carriage with large windows giving passengers better scenery

explanation.surface: A promise of brighter futures for those riding the trains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prospects' suggests career hopes; it means views from a train carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway carriage with big windows built for passengers to enjoy the scenery.

clue.text: See bridal arrangement is what is wanted

indicators.note: an arrangement of the words see and bridal puts their letters in a new order

explanation.surface: A wedding planner looks over the bridal arrangements and approves them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something worth having is wanted, the meaning of the adjective.

clue.text: Breathtaking catches

parts.note: read literally: sharp catches of the breath, each one taking in air suddenly

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator praises some spectacular fielding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breathtaking catches' looks like praise for fielding; read literally they are catches of the breath that take breath in.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden sharp intakes of air are catches in the breath, each literally taking breath.

clue.text: Just a foot — that's the long, and the short of it

definitions.text: Just a foot — that's the long, and the short of it

parts.words: Just a foot — that's the long, and the short of it
parts.note: a metrical foot made of one long syllable followed by one short, playing on the idiom 'the long and the short of it'

explanation.surface: Someone sums up a measurement bluntly: just a foot, and that is all there is to say.
explanation.definitionFit: In verse this metrical foot is a stressed or long syllable followed by an unstressed or short one.

clue.text: Taking a sound correspondence course ?

parts.note: read literally: following a course in which word endings correspond in sound, as in verse

explanation.surface: A student signs up for a reliable course of study by post.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'correspondence course' is study by post; here the correspondence is between sounds of word endings, as in poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Words that end with matching sounds correspond in sound, which is what verse with this feature does.

clue.text: A call for which one holds the cards ?

definitions.text: A call for which one holds the cards

parts.words: A call for which one holds the cards
parts.note: read literally: a social call for which the caller carries calling cards, not playing cards

explanation.surface: A card player's bid made from a strong hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call' and 'holds the cards' suggest bridge or poker; the cards are the visiting cards once left when paying a social call.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying a social call on someone, once done with printed calling cards in hand.

clue.text: What the Baker did after saying " It's a Boo — "

definitions.text: What the Baker did after saying " It's a Boo — "

parts.words: What the Baker did after saying " It's a Boo — "
parts.note: an allusion to Lewis Carroll's The Hunting of the Snark, where the Baker disappears mid-word on finding the Snark is a Boojum

explanation.surface: A baker is startled into silence while saying something spooky.
explanation.walkthrough: In Lewis Carroll's poem The Hunting of the Snark, the Baker cries 'It's a Boo—' and then 'softly and suddenly vanished away', because the Snark was a Boojum.
explanation.definitionFit: The Baker disappeared from sight, as the poem's closing lines describe.

clue.text: Policeman enters: poor shanty of old Greek informer

indicators.note: the policeman enters, going inside the other letters
a poor shanty is a ramshackle one, so its letters are rebuilt

parts.note: a cop is a policeman

explanation.surface: A policeman visits the shack of an informer in ancient Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: The ancient Athenian sense of the word was an informer; 'poor' signals the anagram and 'enters' the insertion.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Athens the word meant an informer before it came to mean a flatterer.

clue.text: Humorist has had it — a walk-on part in radio ?

parts.note: a wag is a joker
someone who has had it is a goner

explanation.surface: A comedian's career is over: reduced to bit parts on the wireless.
explanation.walkthrough: Waggoners' Walk was a BBC radio soap of 1969-80, so a part in it was a 'walk-on' in a Waggoners' Walk.
explanation.definitionFit: A cart driver; also a character in the BBC radio serial Waggoners' Walk.

clue.text: The evil eye, say, taking an embracing view

indicators.note: say marks that the words before it are to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: evil is sin and an eye is optic, so the phrase heard gives sin optic

explanation.surface: Someone fixing a broad gaze is accused of giving the evil eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The evil eye' looks like a superstition; it is SIN (evil) plus OPTIC (eye), which spoken sounds the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A synopsis gives an overall summary, so this adjective describes seeing a subject as a whole.

clue.text: Diminutive CID railway worker ?

definitions.meaning: a detective from Scotland Yard, shortened to the Yard
a worker in a railway yard

explanation.walkthrough: CID is Britain's Criminal Investigation Department, based at Scotland Yard; 'the Yard' is the diminutive, short form.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scotland Yard detective in short form, and someone employed in a railway goods or shunting yard.

clue.text: It's been around since Roman times

definitions.text: It's been around since Roman times

parts.words: It's been around since Roman times
parts.note: read literally: a Latin word meaning 'around' that has survived since the Romans spoke it

explanation.surface: Something very old has existed since the days of ancient Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Been around' suggests longevity; the Latin preposition literally means 'around' and is still used before approximate dates.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin word means about or approximately, used with dates, and came down from the Romans.

clue.text: This, with our domestic pets, making heavy going?

definitions.text: This, with our domestic pets, making heavy going?

parts.words: This, with our domestic pets, making heavy going?
parts.note: the idiom of weather pouring down: add cats and dogs to this word

explanation.surface: Getting about is hard work with our cats and dogs in tow.
explanation.walkthrough: The domestic pets are cats and dogs, completing the idiom for a downpour.
explanation.definitionFit: Precipitation falling heavily, as in the phrase about cats and dogs.

clue.text: A type that gets money — that's tip top!

parts.note: pica is a size of printing type
L stands for pound, a unit of money

explanation.surface: A printer's font earning cash is declared excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip-top' looks like praise; it means at the very tip.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to the apex or tip of something.

clue.text: Wine one firm produced made the columns.

parts.note: port is a fortified wine from Portugal
the Roman numeral for one is I
Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A wine company paid for a colonnade to be built.
explanation.definitionFit: A porch whose roof rests on a row of pillars is a classical colonnaded entrance.

clue.text: Salmi prepared in Mohammedan countries

indicators.note: a salmi is a dish, and preparing it rearranges these letters

explanation.surface: A game stew is cooked in Muslim lands.
explanation.walkthrough: A salmi is a ragout of game birds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muslim world collectively, the lands where the faith is followed.

clue.text: Flier does circuit with RAF formation

parts.note: one circuit of a track is a lap
a wing is a unit of the Royal Air Force

explanation.surface: A pilot flies a circuit alongside an RAF squadron.
explanation.definitionFit: This bird, also called the peewit, is a flier of farmland.

clue.text: It carries me in state

indicators.note: in places the word me inside the abbreviation for the state

parts.note: Cal. is an abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of being borne along in ceremonial splendour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In state' suggests lying in ceremony; here the state is California, abbreviated, with 'me' put inside.
explanation.definitionFit: This desert animal is a beast of burden that carries riders and loads.

clue.text: This way on board, not only for the mate

definitions.meaning: on a ship a ... is the hatch or stair leading below, as in companionway
a mate is a friend or partner

explanation.surface: A sailor shows the way below deck, and not just to the first mate.
explanation.walkthrough: On board ship, the companion (companionway) is the staircase from deck to cabins; 'mate' looks nautical but means a friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's stairway below is the companion ladder, and a friend or partner is someone's comrade.

clue.text: Outstanding feature — unifying sterling and German currency

parts.note: L stands for libra, the pound sterling symbol
and is the word that joins or unites things
the mark was Germany's currency before the euro

explanation.surface: A financier celebrates a deal linking the pound and the Deutschmark.
explanation.definitionFit: A prominent object in the scenery that stands out and guides travellers.

clue.text: The old fellow makes a mess of "Greats"

indicators.note: making a mess of the word Greats jumbles its letters

explanation.surface: An elderly Oxford man flunks his classics finals.
explanation.walkthrough: Greats is the Oxford classics degree; an 'old stager' is a veteran.
explanation.definitionFit: An old stager is a veteran, someone long experienced.
